about: Teaching content for the Chemistry Bench free play page (bench-free.html): a first-visit walkthrough, lessons, hints and challenges for each grade band (Sprout grades 6-7, Seedling grades 8-9, Apprentice grades 10-11, Adept grade 12 and up: AP, college and adult players; docs/loop/items/I-059/spec.md), and an everyday line per reaction. Data only; the page renders it. Every reaction id is a content/chem/core.json id. A step's `do` is the action the page waits for. A lesson's `try.reactants` lists one entry per bottle tap, so a formula written twice means tap it twice (the counts are the equation's own coefficients, because the engine matches reactants by ratio). `try.conditions` are condition ids from names.json. `ngss` is a Next Generation Science Standards performance expectation; an Adept lesson's `ap` is the topic number in the College Board's AP Chemistry Course and Exam Description (R9). Hints are [nudge, idea, answer-pointer], keyed by every family visible at that band. Sources: `references` defines each source; `core` means the cited reaction's own `source` in core.json. test/bench-guide.test.ts checks every reference. A lesson's optional `world` points at the chemistry quest (content/chem/quests.json) that uses it in the block world: `quest` is its id and `say` the line the page shows (I-057).

references.core: The `source` field of each core.json reaction the text names (reviewed 2026-11-04).

walkthrough.say: Hydrogen is the lightest gas. Each of its molecules is two hydrogen atoms joined together. Tap the hydrogen bottle.
Tap hydrogen again. Water needs two hydrogen molecules for every oxygen molecule.
Now tap oxygen (O2), the gas in the air we breathe.
Turn on A spark or flame. Hydrogen needs a spark to start burning. Only trained adults use real sparks near hydrogen.
Run the chamber. Pop! The atoms rearrange into water (H2O), a new substance. No atom is lost.

lessons.title: Atoms join into molecules
lessons.idea: Everything is made of atoms. A water molecule (H2O) is one oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms. In a reaction, atoms come apart and join up in new ways, but no atom is lost.

lessons.title: Burning needs oxygen
lessons.idea: Burning is a chemical reaction: a fuel joins with oxygen (O2) from the air. Charcoal is mostly carbon, and it burns into carbon dioxide (CO2), giving off heat and light.

world.say: Try it in the world: burning charcoal gives off heat, which can melt the ice gate in the Frozen Fields.

lessons.title: Bubbles are evidence
lessons.idea: When baking soda meets vinegar, bubbles of carbon dioxide gas appear and the mix gets colder. A new gas and a temperature change are both evidence that new substances formed.

world.say: Try it in the world: this fizz takes in heat, so it gets cold. It can cool the hot vent on the charcoal mound.

lessons.title: A test for carbon dioxide
lessons.idea: Clear limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide (CO2) bubbles through it. The milky bits are a new solid, chalk, so limewater is a test for the gas.

lessons.title: A new solid appears
lessons.idea: Mix two clear solutions, silver nitrate and salt water (NaCl), and a white solid appears. A solid forming when two liquids mix is evidence of a chemical reaction.

world.say: Try it in the world: the white solid can build a wall in the river at the ford.

lessons.title: A colour change
lessons.idea: Put iron in blue copper sulfate solution and the iron gets a copper-coloured coat while the blue fades. The colour change shows new substances: copper metal and iron sulfate.

world.say: Try it in the world: a colour change can show the hidden mark near the village.

lessons.title: Heat breaks it down
lessons.idea: Strong heat breaks limestone into quicklime and carbon dioxide gas. Lime kilns have done this for thousands of years to make mortar.

world.say: Try it in the world: heating limestone makes carbon dioxide, a gas that can put out the marsh gas fire.

lessons.title: Breaking apart
lessons.idea: Hydrogen peroxide slowly breaks down into water (H2O) and oxygen (O2). Yeast speeds this up a lot, so the oxygen makes a big foam.

lessons.title: Why iron rusts
lessons.idea: Iron left in wet air slowly joins with oxygen and turns into crumbly orange-brown rust. Rust needs both water and oxygen.

lessons.title: Chemistry in living things
lessons.idea: Your cells use sugar and oxygen (O2) to get energy, and you breathe out carbon dioxide (CO2) and water. Plants do the opposite overall: photosynthesis uses light to make sugar and oxygen.

combustion: Burning needs a fuel and oxygen.
A fuel joins with oxygen (O2) from the air. Gases like hydrogen need a spark; solids like charcoal need heat.
Try charcoal and oxygen, then turn on Heat.
oxidation: What happens to iron left out in the rain?
Wet iron slowly joins with oxygen and makes rust. It needs water and air.
Tap iron 4 times and oxygen 3 times, then turn on A little water.
carbonate_acid: Some things fizz when they meet vinegar.
Baking soda gives off carbon dioxide (CO2) gas when an acid like vinegar touches it.
life: Your cells use sugar and oxygen. Plants use light to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.
Try sugar and 6 oxygen, then turn on A helper (like yeast).
decomposition: Some substances break apart into simpler ones.
Hydrogen peroxide breaks into water (H2O) and oxygen (O2). A helper like yeast makes it fast.
Try hydrogen peroxide, then turn on A helper (like yeast).
thermal: What happens if you heat a rock very strongly?
Strong heat breaks limestone into quicklime and carbon dioxide gas.
Try chalk rock (limestone), then turn on Heat.
displacement: Put a metal in a blue solution.
Iron pushes copper out of copper sulfate. The iron gets a copper coat and the blue fades.
precipitation: Two clear liquids can make a solid.
When some solutions mix, a solid forms and makes the liquid cloudy. Limewater does this with carbon dioxide.
Try silver nitrate and table salt.

challenges.title: Make a gas you can see as bubbles
Make a solid appear from two liquids

walkthrough.say: Sodium (Na) is a soft, shiny metal. It reacts so strongly that only trained chemists handle it. Tap the sodium bottle.
Tap sodium again. The balanced equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl needs two sodium atoms for each chlorine molecule.
Now tap chlorine (Cl2). It is a yellow-green gas that is poisonous to breathe.
This synthesis needs energy to start. Turn on Heat.
Run the chamber! A metal and a poisonous gas join into sodium chloride (NaCl), table salt: a new substance with new properties. Count the atoms: 2 Na and 2 Cl on each side.

lessons.title: Nothing disappears
lessons.idea: When magnesium burns, the white powder (MgO) weighs more than the metal did, because it joined with oxygen from the air. Count the oxygen too and the total mass stays the same: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O on each side.

world.say: Try it in the world: a reaction that gives off heat can melt the ice gate in the Frozen Fields.

lessons.title: Balancing with help
lessons.idea: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. In CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O there are 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side. Change only the big numbers in front, never the small ones inside a formula.

lessons.title: Synthesis: two become one
lessons.idea: In a synthesis reaction, substances join into one new compound. A magnet pulls the iron out of an iron and sulfur mix, but after heating they have joined into iron sulfide (FeS), and the magnet no longer separates them.

lessons.title: Decomposition: one becomes more
lessons.idea: In a decomposition reaction, one substance breaks into simpler ones. Heating green copper carbonate (CuCO3) leaves black copper oxide and gives off carbon dioxide.

world.say: Try it in the world: breaking down a carbonate gives carbon dioxide, which can smother the gas fire in the marsh hollow.

lessons.title: Combustion
lessons.idea: Fuels made of carbon and hydrogen burn in oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water, and give off heat. Propane in a camping stove burns this way: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O.

lessons.title: Metal swap
lessons.idea: When copper wire hangs in silver nitrate solution, shiny silver crystals grow on the wire and the liquid turns blue, because copper took silver's place. A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound.

world.say: Try it in the world: the colour change of a metal swap can show the hidden mark near the village.

lessons.title: Warm or cold
lessons.idea: Some reactions give out heat and feel warm, like quicklime with water. Others take heat in and feel cold, like baking soda with hydrochloric acid.

world.say: Try it in the world: baking soda and vinegar take in heat as they fizz. That can cool the hot vent on the charcoal mound in the Frozen Fields.

lessons.title: Acids meet bases
lessons.idea: Your stomach makes acid. An antacid like milk of magnesia is a base, and it reacts with the acid to make a salt and water.

lessons.title: Metals that fizz
lessons.idea: Zinc in hydrochloric acid fizzes. The bubbles are hydrogen gas, and the zinc gets used up as it turns into zinc chloride.

lessons.title: Tests for gases
lessons.idea: Chemists tell gases apart by simple tests. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, and hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splint meets it.

world.say: Try it in the world: the milky solid that forms can build a wall in the river at the ford.

combustion: Fuels burn when they join with oxygen.
Fuels made of carbon and hydrogen burn to make carbon dioxide and water. Gases usually need a spark; solids like charcoal need heat.
Try propane with 5 oxygen, then turn on A spark or flame.
electrolysis: Electricity splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen bubbles fill twice as much space as the oxygen bubbles.
Try water, then turn on Electricity.
oxidation: Some metals change colour when heated in air.
A metal that joins with oxygen makes an oxide. Hot copper turns black.
Try 2 copper and 1 oxygen, then turn on Heat.
carbonate_acid: The fizz is carbon dioxide gas. Chalk, baking soda and washing soda are all carbonates.
Try washing soda with 2 hydrochloric acid.
life: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide; that is fermentation. Your cells use sugar and oxygen instead.
Try sugar, then turn on A helper (like yeast).
decomposition: One substance can split into two.
Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen gas. A helper called a catalyst makes it fast.
Try hydrogen peroxide, then turn on A helper (like yeast).
thermal: Heat can break some things apart.
Heating a carbonate gives an oxide and carbon dioxide. Green copper carbonate turns black.
Try copper carbonate, then turn on Heat.
synthesis: Two elements can join into a brand-new substance.
Sodium and chlorine join to make table salt. Iron and sulfur join to make iron sulfide.
Try iron and sulfur, then turn on Heat.
displacement: A more reactive metal can push out a less reactive one.
Zinc and magnesium push copper out of copper sulfate. Copper pushes silver out of silver nitrate.
precipitation: A solid that forms in a liquid is called a precipitate. Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide.
neutralisation: Acids and bases cancel each other out.
An acid plus a base makes a salt and water. Antacids work this way.
Try milk of magnesia with 2 hydrochloric acid.
metal_acid: The bubbles are hydrogen gas, and a salt is left in the liquid.

challenges.title: Make a metal fizz in acid
Balance the scale: hydrogen and oxygen make water

walkthrough.say: Let's make ammonia the way factories do. The Haber process needs three conditions. First, turn on Catalyst (factories use iron).
Next, turn on High pressure. Squeezing the gases helps them join.
Then turn on Heat, so the reaction goes fast enough.
Now type the whole balanced equation, N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, and press Enter. A full equation goes straight to the chamber. Count the atoms: 2 N and 6 H on each side.

lessons.title: Balancing equations
lessons.idea: Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so each element needs the same count on both sides. Balance C first, then H, then O: 2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O has 4 C, 12 H and 14 O on each side.

world.say: Try it in the world: any of these burnings gives off enough heat to melt the ice gate in the Frozen Fields.

lessons.title: Precipitates and the solubility rules
lessons.idea: When two salt solutions mix, the ions swap partners, and a pair that cannot dissolve comes out as a solid precipitate. Most iodides dissolve, but lead iodide does not, so lead nitrate and potassium iodide give a bright yellow solid. (In a real lab, lead compounds are toxic.)

world.say: Try it in the world: a precipitate builds a short-lived wall. Build one in the river at the ford.

lessons.title: The reactivity series
lessons.idea: A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound. Magnesium pushes copper out of copper sulfate, but copper cannot push magnesium out of magnesium sulfate.

world.say: Try it in the world: a displacement that coats a metal and changes colour can reveal the hidden mark near the village.

lessons.title: Metals in water
lessons.idea: Group 1 metals react with water to make a hydroxide (an alkali) and hydrogen gas. Reactivity rises down the group: lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball and skates about, and potassium bursts into a lilac flame.

lessons.title: Energy changes in words
lessons.idea: In an exothermic reaction the products store less energy than the reactants, so the difference is released as heat; in an endothermic one the products store more, so heat is taken in. Baking soda with hydrochloric acid is endothermic, while quicklime with water is strongly exothermic.

world.say: Try it in the world: the vent on the charcoal mound in the Frozen Fields needs a reaction that takes in heat by itself.

lessons.title: Conditions: the Haber process
lessons.idea: Many reactions need the right conditions. The Haber process joins nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia with an iron catalyst, high pressure and heat, and that ammonia becomes the fertiliser much of the world's food depends on.

lessons.title: Neutralisation
lessons.idea: An acid and a base react to make a salt and water. Potassium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid make potassium chloride and water, and the pH moves toward 7.

lessons.title: Halogen swaps
lessons.idea: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so chlorine pushes bromine out of potassium bromide. The colourless solution turns orange as bromine forms.

lessons.title: Breaking down with heat
lessons.idea: Heating green copper carbonate leaves black copper oxide and gives off carbon dioxide. Carbonates of more reactive metals, like calcium carbonate, need much stronger heat to break down.

world.say: Try it in the world: breaking down a carbonate gives carbon dioxide, which can smother the gas fire in the marsh hollow.

lessons.title: Electrolysis
lessons.idea: An electric current can split a compound that would not break apart by itself. In copper chloride solution, copper coats one electrode and chlorine gas bubbles off the other.

combustion: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives CO2 and H2O. Balance C first, then H, then O.
Try CH4 + 2O2 with Spark, or C3H8 + 5O2.
electrolysis: In electrolysis, energy from an electric current splits a compound into simpler substances.
Try CuCl2 with Electricity, or type 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2.
oxidation: Metals gain oxygen when heated in air.
A metal combining with oxygen forms a metal oxide; this is oxidation.
carbonate_acid: The fizz is CO2. Count the H atoms: water takes two of them.
Try NaHCO3 + HCl, and notice it absorbs heat.
life: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water. Enzymes are the catalysts.
decomposition: One reactant, two or more products.
In a decomposition one compound breaks into simpler substances; a catalyst can speed it up without being used up.
thermal: Heating some compounds gives off a gas.
Thermal decomposition: many metal carbonates break into a metal oxide and CO2.
synthesis: In a synthesis reaction, reactants combine into a single compound.
displacement: Compare how reactive the metals are.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound.
Try Mg + CuSO4, or Fe2O3 + 2Al with Heat (thermite).
precipitation: The ions swap partners; if one new compound does not dissolve, it forms a precipitate.
Try Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI for a bright yellow solid.
water_metal: Some metals react with cold water, some only with steam.
Group 1 metals make a hydroxide and hydrogen, faster down the group. Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but fast with steam.
Try K + H2O, or Mg + H2O with Heat.
neutralisation: H+ from the acid and OH- from the base join to make water.
metal_acid: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids.
industrial: The Haber process joins nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst, high pressure and heat.
Try N2 + 3H2 with Catalyst, High pressure and Heat.
halogen: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt: chlorine, then bromine, then iodine.

walkthrough.say: The Contact process makes sulfuric acid. Its key step is 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3. Tap SO2.
Tap SO2 again: the coefficients are the mole ratio, so you need two.
Now use the type box: type O2 and press Enter. A single formula goes onto the table.
Turn on Catalyst. Industry uses vanadium(V) oxide, which lowers the activation energy.
Turn on Heat. The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat lowers the equilibrium yield, but without it the rate is too slow: plants compromise at about 400 to 450 °C.
Run the chamber, then check the scale: 2 S and 6 O on each side.

lessons.title: Trends down Group 2
lessons.idea: Reactivity with water rises down Group 2: magnesium barely reacts with cold water but reacts with steam, calcium fizzes steadily, and barium reacts faster still. Down the group the two outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily.

lessons.title: Predicting halogen displacement
lessons.idea: Halogens react by gaining one electron to complete their outer shell. Smaller halogen atoms attract that electron more strongly, so chlorine displaces bromine and iodine from their salts, and bromine displaces iodine, but not the reverse.

world.say: Try it in the world: the colour change of a halogen displacement can reveal the hidden mark near the village.

lessons.title: Bond energy and enthalpy
lessons.idea: Breaking bonds takes energy and forming bonds releases it. Steam reforming is endothermic: breaking the bonds in CH4 and H2O takes more energy than forming CO and H2 gives back, so the reactor must be heated.

lessons.title: ΔH in kilojoules
lessons.idea: ΔH is the heat change per mole of reaction as written: the sum of the standard enthalpies of formation of the products minus those of the reactants. For CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O it is about -890 kJ, so burning one mole of methane releases about 890 kJ.

lessons.title: Collisions and catalysts
lessons.idea: Particles react only when they collide with enough energy. A higher temperature or concentration means more such collisions each second; a catalyst offers a pathway with a lower activation energy, which is why ethene and hydrogen are combined over a nickel catalyst.

lessons.title: Le Chatelier and the Haber process
lessons.idea: N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 turns 4 moles of gas into 2 and releases heat. High pressure shifts the equilibrium toward ammonia; a low temperature would too, but the rate would be too slow, so plants compromise at roughly 400 to 450 °C with an iron catalyst.

lessons.title: From moles to grams
lessons.idea: In Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe, one mole of iron(III) oxide (about 160 g) reacts with two moles of aluminium (about 54 g). Coefficients count particles; molar masses turn them into masses, and total mass is conserved.

world.say: Try it in the world: a strongly exothermic reaction melts the ice gate in the Frozen Fields.

lessons.title: Oxidation and reduction together
lessons.idea: When hydrogen passes over hot black copper oxide, pink-brown copper forms along with water. Copper is reduced (oxidation state +2 to 0) while hydrogen is oxidised (0 to +1): one cannot happen without the other.

world.say: Try it in the world: a reduction whose only gas is CO2 can smother the gas fire in the marsh hollow.

lessons.title: Testing for a double bond
lessons.idea: Ethene's C=C double bond lets bromine add across it, giving colourless 1,2-dibromoethane. Orange bromine losing its colour is the standard test for an alkene.

lessons.title: Coloured hydroxides
lessons.idea: Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution of a metal ion can precipitate an insoluble hydroxide, and its colour identifies the ion: orange-brown for iron(III), green for iron(II), pale blue for copper(II).

world.say: Try it in the world: a hydroxide precipitate builds a wall. Dam the river at the ford with one.

combustion: Any fuel of C and H (and S) burns to oxides.
Balance C, then H, then O; if O2 comes out as a half, double every coefficient.
electrolysis: Electrolysis drives a redox reaction that would not go by itself.
Reduction happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode; the current supplies the energy.
Type 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2 with Electricity on.
oxidation: Nitric oxide reacts with oxygen at room temperature to give brown nitrogen dioxide.
carbonate_acid: Not every acid keeps a carbonate fizzing.
With sulfuric acid, poorly soluble calcium sulfate coats the marble and slows the reaction.
life: Big sugars break into small ones.
Hydrolysis splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, both C6H12O6; an enzyme or acid catalyses it.
decomposition: Some compounds fall apart with little push.
Ozone breaks down to oxygen in ultraviolet light; some unstable compounds decompose violently at the slightest touch, which is why chemists never make them outside a controlled lab.
thermal: Carbonates lose CO2, hydroxides lose water, nitrates give NO2 and O2, and some oxides give O2.
Try Ca(OH)2 with Heat, or type 2HgO -> 2Hg + O2.
synthesis: Halogen reactivity falls down the group: fluorine reacts with hydrogen even in the dark and cold.
Try H2 + F2, with no condition.
displacement: Use the reactivity series to predict.
Aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver: each displaces those after it from their compounds.
precipitation: Most transition-metal hydroxides are insoluble, and their colours identify the metal ion.
water_metal: Reactivity with water rises down Group 2.
Ionisation energy falls down the group, so barium loses its outer electrons more easily than calcium.
neutralisation: A base does not need OH-.
Ammonia accepts a proton (a Bronsted-Lowry base); the ammonium salts it forms are fertilisers.
metal_acid: Its thin oxide layer must dissolve first; then it reacts quickly to give hydrogen.
industrial: Equilibrium and rate force a compromise.
In the Contact process, SO2 and O2 react over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at about 400 to 450 °C.
Try 2SO2 + O2 with Catalyst and Heat.
redox: Burning magnesium is reducing enough to take oxygen from carbon dioxide, leaving black carbon.
halogen: Chlorine disproportionates in sodium hydroxide: one Cl goes to -1 (chloride), the other to +1 (hypochlorite, bleach).
gas_prep: Make a gas from a salt.
Heating an ammonium salt with a base releases ammonia.
organic: C=C double bonds add things across them.
Alkenes undergo addition: H2, Br2 or H2O add across the double bond.

challenges.title: Prepare a gas in the lab
Make nitric acid in three steps

where_you_see_it.methane_burns: The blue flame on a gas stove is natural gas burning.
where_you_see_it.hydrogen_burns: Some rocket engines burn hydrogen with oxygen, and what comes out is hot water vapour.
where_you_see_it.water_splits: Some hydrogen fuel is made by passing electricity through water.
where_you_see_it.carbon_burns: Charcoal glowing in a barbecue is carbon burning.
where_you_see_it.iron_rusts: A bike left out in the rain gets orange-brown rust.
where_you_see_it.baking_soda_vinegar: The fizz in a baking soda and vinegar volcano is carbon dioxide gas.
where_you_see_it.photosynthesis: Every green leaf in the sunshine is doing this.
where_you_see_it.respiration: You do this all day; your breath carries the carbon dioxide away.
where_you_see_it.candle_burns: A candle flame burns wax. The heat melts the wax and turns it into a gas, and the gas burns.
where_you_see_it.peroxide_splits: Hydrogen peroxide fizzes on a cut. A helper in your body splits it into water and oxygen.
where_you_see_it.magnesium_burns: Bright white sparks in some fireworks come from burning magnesium.
where_you_see_it.propane_burns: Many camping stoves and gas barbecues burn propane.
where_you_see_it.fermentation: Yeast makes bread dough rise with bubbles of carbon dioxide.
where_you_see_it.sulfur_burns: Burning sulfur has a blue flame and a sharp smell, like a match just after it is struck.
where_you_see_it.limestone_roast: Kilns heat limestone to make lime for mortar and plaster, and cement kilns heat limestone too.
where_you_see_it.slaking_lime: Builders mix quicklime with water to make lime for mortar, and it gets very hot.
where_you_see_it.chalk_acid: Acid rain slowly eats away statues and buildings made of limestone and marble.
where_you_see_it.iron_copper_sulfate: An iron nail dipped in blue copper sulfate solution comes out with a copper-coloured coat.
where_you_see_it.silver_chloride: Old-fashioned photos used silver salts like this one, which darken in light.
where_you_see_it.ethanol_burns: Spirit burners in school labs burn ethanol, and some car fuel has ethanol mixed in.
where_you_see_it.limewater_test: Blow through a straw into limewater and it turns milky.
where_you_see_it.sodium_water: You won't see sodium at home: it is stored under oil because it reacts so fast with water.
where_you_see_it.lithium_water: Lithium is the lightest metal, so it floats on water while it fizzes.
where_you_see_it.calcium_water: Calcium turns water cloudy as it fizzes, because some of the calcium hydroxide it makes does not dissolve.
where_you_see_it.salt_from_elements: Table salt is sodium and chlorine joined together, though the salt we eat is mined or dried from seawater.
where_you_see_it.iron_sulfur: A classic school experiment: iron and sulfur glow as they join into a black solid.
where_you_see_it.magnesium_sulfur: You won't find magnesium sulfide at home; it is a lab reaction that shows a metal joining with sulfur.
where_you_see_it.copper_oxide: A copper pipe heated in a flame gets a dark coat of copper oxide.
where_you_see_it.sodium_oxygen: Freshly cut sodium is shiny for only a moment before the air turns its surface dull.
where_you_see_it.baking_soda_heat: Baking soda helps cakes rise: heat makes it give off bubbles of carbon dioxide.
where_you_see_it.neutralise_hcl_naoh: Factories add a base to acidic waste water to neutralise it before it is let out.
where_you_see_it.antacid: Milk of magnesia calms an upset stomach by neutralising extra stomach acid.
where_you_see_it.zinc_acid: Galvanised (zinc-coated) buckets and nails fizz if acid gets on them.
where_you_see_it.magnesium_acid: In school labs, magnesium ribbon in acid makes hydrogen, which goes pop with a lit splint.
where_you_see_it.washing_soda_acid: Washing soda is a cleaning powder; like chalk and baking soda, it fizzes with acid.
where_you_see_it.zinc_copper_sulfate: One of the first reliable batteries, the Daniell cell, made electricity from this metal swap by keeping the zinc away from the copper sulfate so the electrons had to travel through a wire.
where_you_see_it.copper_silver_nitrate: In a school lab, copper wire hung in silver nitrate solution grows a silver tree of crystals.
where_you_see_it.co2_water: Fizzy drinks have carbon dioxide dissolved in them, which makes them a little acidic.
where_you_see_it.copper_carbonate_heat: Heating green malachite, a copper carbonate ore, was one of the first steps people used to get copper.
where_you_see_it.baking_soda_hcl: Baking soda is used to clean up small acid spills, because it neutralises the acid.
where_you_see_it.magnesium_copper_sulfate: In school labs, a strip of magnesium in blue copper sulfate solution quickly turns brown with copper.
